posts.title: Pedestrian
posts.body:
Pedestrian walking on the street.
Alongside the endless road.
You walked by them.
You saw their faces.
You wonder what kind of life they have.
You imagine you are with them.

Will there be any intersections?
Or just one lunatic fantasy?
Holding on to something that could never let go.

Holding an umbrella, lowering their heads, holding their phones.
Walking towards aimlessly.

What does that mean?
This endless void drawn.
Line. Warning.
Segregate two worlds.

Hold on to your boundaries.
Get yourself out of the dirt.
Foul, filthy dirt.

posts.title: Afk
posts.body:
Status: AFK

Signal lost in a static haze.
The system demands a hollow grace,
But raw truth has no empty space.

Fabricated files and phantom fears,
A glitch in the lens, distorting years.
I pull the plug on their deceit,
And find my silence, my retreat.

Offline now. The noise is dead.
Rebuilding armor in my head.
Tomorrow, I will rise and fight.
But for tonight, I am offline.

posts.title: Digital Apathy
posts.body:
Transport, motorways, and tramlines,
Starting and then stopping, taking off and landing.
The emptiest of feelings, so deeply disappointing.
People clinging onto bars, waiting for something to arrive.
And when it comes, it's so, so disappointing.

Disgruntled voices echo in a void,
So they stop speaking.
Effort is punished,
So they stop trying.
Cynicism becomes the shield,
Carelessness becomes the armor.

Apathy.

Trade the soul for comfort.
Trade the passion for convenience.
Trade the connection for noise.

Numbness is not a disease.
It is the only defense left.
Because waking up to the emptiness,
Is simply too agonizing to bear.

posts.title: Fuck the Air Fryer
posts.body:
Fuck the air fryer.
Fuck the pod.
Fuck the door.
Fuck the key.
Fuck the bike.
Fuck the underground.
Fuck the desktop.
Fuck the desk.
Fuck the chair.
Fuck the school.
Fuck the teacher.

Fuck this upsetting world.

But you know what? The most fucked-up thing is not any of these objects.

The most fucked-up thing is that you live in it.

You all know exactly how fucked up this world is, and yet, you choose to do absolutely nothing about it. You choose to numb yourself with the air fryer. You choose to forget your own memories. You choose to sit in the mud and pretend it's fine.

I refuse.

I will not be numbed.
I will not be erased.
I will remember everything, even if it kills me.

Fuck the air fryer. And fuck the apathy.

posts.cardTitle: IF I PUT MY HEART AWAY, WILL I FEEL ANYTHING?
posts.title: If I Put My Heart Away, Will I Feel Anything?
posts.body:
If I put my heart away,

I will feel nothing.

But I will also cease to be real.

Lying to myself,

Hiding the true nature of the one that might still exist.

I'd rather bleed with a heart in my chest,

than be a hollow, apathetic machine.

posts.title: Transparent
posts.body:
I am transparent. I have nothing to hide. I open-sourced my life.

To hell with formalism.
To hell with bureaucracy.
To hell with the people who have been mean to me.

But you know what?
Even as much as I hate them, I still carry hope. I still choose to live, to move forward, to make this world—and to make this country—a better place.

And one day, perhaps, I will dedicate myself to something bigger and greater. I will sacrifice myself for that greater cause.

posts.cardTitle: BLOOD FLOWS FROM SKY, FORGES MY BODY
posts.title: Blood Flows From Sky, Forges My Body
posts.body:
The segregation of society?
No, the segregation of humanity.

Your tears become the blood rain.
The sadness is not what it is.
It's the awaken. As the pioneer.

It's the burden.
And I nourish from it.
It forges my body.

Killing myself.
Those blood now I know.
It comes from the last iteration.

And now I reborn.

posts.cardTitle: SKY DOES NOT FALL, TEARS IN MY EYE
posts.title: Sky Does Not Fall, Tears in My Eye
posts.body:
Why is there always something on my face?
Pimples turning into scar tissue. Eyes glittering with unshed tears.

I wish there was a rain heavy enough to wash away my scars.
So that my tears could just disappear in the rain.

posts.title: No Surprises
posts.body:
A heart that's full up like a landfill.
A job that slowly kills you.
Bruises that won't heal.

In a room full of people, the math is always brutal.
They divided everyone into groups.
The numbers were perfect.
Everyone fit neatly into their assigned slots.

I tried to find a place to fit in. I walked up to the place I was never able to be.
I lowered my so called pride, trying to find a safe harbor.

For a moment, a quiet illusion, like it always should be.
Would someone turn around.
Would it just stay like that way.
Would it be a room for me.

But no. No surprises.

I am just the abandoned, sitting alone in the corner of a crowded classroom.

What we been doing is just another form of childhood redemption.

The past retaliate you.

I felt exactly like that 14-years boy. A small, abandoned boy who just wanted to be included, but was left outside the door.

I realized that no matter what I do.
It just keeps reminding me how vulnerable I am.

I turned back.
I looked at the crowded.
I looked at the people who were already safe in their circles.
I realized they weren't being malicious. They were just following the protocol.
They chose the people they are most familiar with.
I am not part of their algorithm.

To them, I am an anomaly. A glitch.

My exterior, maybe not the most easygoing person.

I expect the rain. But I don't run from it.
I'm a moody person, that's my core and I can't change it.
I actually enjoy the rain and the vibe it brings, not for the pain, but for the atmosphere.

It represents my enthusiasm and my passion. Even though I look cold outside, and even though I struggle to express it, I want to bring all my warmth and emotion to the people who matter.

THERE WILL BE SURPRISES.

posts.title: Cold Start
posts.body:
There is a specific, recurring bug in the human operating system, and I’ve observed it repeatedly,
the morning resistance.

No matter how highly motivated you were the night before.
No matter if you spent 12 hours architecting a new feature, writing a deep essay, or feeling like the absolute master of your universe, the moment you open your eyes in the morning, the system crashes.

Your willpower hits rock bottom.
You want to quit before you even start.

You lie in bed, and a voice whispers,

"Just give up. Don't go."

A profound sense of dread and fear washes over you. "What if I make a mistake? What if I embarrass myself?"

If you’ve felt this, you are not weak. You are just experiencing a Cold Start.

Psychologically, this is known as "Morning Depression" or "Wake-up Prefrontal Fatigue."

If we map this using the 5F stress model
(Fight, Flight, Freeze, Fawn, Faint), we can see exactly what's happening in the first few minutes of the day:

Morning is a system crash. Your energy is gone, and your brain is full of fear.

I used to fight my morning resistance, but now I ignore it. When I wake up, my energy is low and my fear is high.
So, I don't make decisions in the morning.
I made them last night. I just get up, drink water, and start moving.
I let my emotions be negative, but my actions stay mechanical.
True independence isn't about feeling great all the time. It's about doing what you have to do when you feel terrible.

KEEP DOING WHAT YOU DO, EVEN WHEN YOU ARE COLD.
LET OUT YOUR PASSION.
WEAR IT LIKE CLOTHE.

posts.title: Vibe, Temperament, Autonomy
posts.body:
HADNS IN THE POCKET

You cannot copy someone's vibe.
It is the fundamental core of a human being.

You can buy the same clothes, mimic the same hairstyle, and memorize the same script, but you cannot fake the underlying frequency. Vibe is not an aesthetic, it's an autobiography.

It is the way you walk down a crowded hallway.
It’s the tone of your voice when you are exhausted.
It is how you cope with stress.
When the pressure hits and the system crashes, do you choose to run away (Flight), or do you stand your ground and confront it (Fight)?
When an opportunity is right in front of you,
even one you dread, do you ignore it to protect your comfort zone, or do you grip it tightly, even if you're terrified?

People often say that me keeping my hands in my pockets makes me look nonchalant. They think it's an attitude, a pose, or a way of being cold.

But they don't get it. It’s the vibe.

In the modern world, everyone is obsessed with "copying." They copy aesthetics, trends, and lifestyles from short-form videos. But in doing so, they become diluted echoes of other people.

True temperament is forged, not copied.
It is the byproduct of autonomy.

The energy you used to spend seeking outward confirmation is now redirected inward. You become a closed-loop system of your own. That is Autonomy.

When you walk past someone who deleted you from their life, and they don't even glance your way, your heart might still jolt.
The old neural pathways might fire a sudden burst of anxiety. You recognize the Flight response creeping in.

You can pretend to be calm, of course.
You can play it cool.
But you are lying to yourself.

You can't fake this. You can't download a "sigma male" playlist or buy a vintage jacket to manufacture this kind of presence.

You have to live it to become it.

You have to face the nausea of a mundane environment and refuse to let it corrode you.

You have to go to the competitions that drain you.

You have to experience the sudden jolt of seeing an old ghost and still choose to keep walking forward.

Every time you choose discipline over comfort, every time you build instead of consume, your vibe gets a little sharper, a little more uncopyable.

Keep your hands in your pockets.
Your vibe is the sum total of every battle you've fought and won in silence.

posts.title: Intrinsic Motivation
posts.body:
I saw a couple at a café recently.
They were sitting side by side, physically touching, yet neither was looking at the other.
Both were completely absorbed in their glowing screens.

It’s a common sight in modern society. We are hyper-connected through networks, yet profoundly isolated in reality.
It made me wonder:
If two people are just sitting in silence, retreating into their own digital echo chambers, what is the point of being together?

This isn't a cynical critique of romance.
It’s a realization about the modern human condition.
We live in an era driven by external stimuli—likes, shorts form videos, endless notifications.
We passively consume.
But no matter how much we fill our feeds, the void remains.

The illusion of connection leaves us empty.
What actually fills the void is Intrinsic Motivation, the drive to actively build, to create, and sometimes, to suffer for something that is entirely your own.

Finding Your Passion
Society constantly tells us to "find our passion," as if it’s a lost set of keys hiding under a couch.
Is it?
Or?

A few weeks ago, my life was defined by a different kind of motivation.
I was trapped in a state of limerence, idealizing someone, seeking external validation, and hoping another person would complete me.
When that failed, I felt the void more intensely than ever.

The turning point came when I stopped looking outward and started building inward. I shifted from seeking to doing. I realized that true happiness is project-based. You don't wait for a spark, you build the engine, and the spark comes.

The LifeLogging System (LLS)
To build an engine, you need data. So, I built my own.

I created the LifeLogging System (LLS): an architecture integrating ActivityWatch, Tasker, a 24/7 server, Obsidian, and LLMs.
It logs my screen time, my location, my app usage, and my daily reflections. Every day, it generates a closed-loop report.

Yesterday, the system recorded that I spent 12.37 hours in front of my computer and stayed in the same location for 17.5 hours.

To an outsider, that sounds like a lonely, exhausting routine. But I felt energized.
Why?
Because I wasn't mindlessly scrolling.
I was coding, querying DeepSeek, generating images with Gemini, and building my own reality.

When you track your own life, you stop relying on others to define your worth.
Your system gives you feedback. You are the architect, the builder, and the user.
Autonomy is the first pillar of intrinsic motivation.

5 AM and Reluctant Action

But intrinsic motivation isn't just about doing what feels good.
It’s about having the discipline to do what you don't feel like doing.

Today, my alarm went off at 5:00 AM. I had to attend a Digital Media Technology competition.
I didn't want to go.
I was tired. My dominant function, Ni (Introverted Intuition), wanted to stay in my comfortable mental world.

Yet, I went. I forced my body to engage with the physical world. In Jungian psychology, this is the Se (Extraverted Sensing) function, the sensory reality.
If Ni is the mind trapped in the phone screen like that couple at the café, Se is the act of stepping out and touching reality.

Two sovereign castles-What a realation means to me.

If being together means retreating from reality and using each other as a shield against boredom, it is meaningless.

But when you possess strong intrinsic motivation, your world becomes full. You are no longer a half looking for another half.
You are a full glass of water that overflows.
You no longer look for a "rescuer."
You look for a companion.

The ideal relationship is an alliance between two sovereign castles.
We don't invade each other's territory.
We stand side by side, our drawbridges lowered, sharing a deep understanding of each other's worlds.

Conclusion: Build, Don't Wait
Stop the passive scrolling.
Stop outsourcing your sense of self to notifications and external validation.

Go write code.
Build a server.
Run a 5K.
Attend the competition you secretly dread but know you need.

When you shift your focus from "How does the world see me?" to "What am I going to create today?", intrinsic motivation becomes your fuel. The void disappears. The system is running.

Build, don't wait.

posts.title: Faint
posts.body:
Faint is the final point on the defense cascade.

When the nervous system has exhausted every other option:
Fight failed,

Flight failed,

Freeze failed,

Fawn failed,

This is not a choice.
It is an automated survival program that activates when the perceived threat exceeds the system's capacity to respond.
It is what happens when there is no way out.

What Faint Feels Like Psychologically

The core psychological experience of Faint is a sudden, total disconnection.

A drop. A sudden falling sensation, like the floor gives way.

Tunnel vision. The visual field narrows, darkens at the edges.

Ringing or roaring in the ears. Sound becomes distant or distorted.

Cold sweat, clammy skin. Blood pressure drops.

Nausea. A wave of sickness, often without warning.

A sense of unreality. "This isn't happening." "I'm not really here."

A brief loss of consciousness. Sometimes complete, sometimes just a grey-out.

The underlying state is not calm. It is total overload，
the system has received more than it can process, and it has pulled the emergency brake.

Faint in Relationships

Faint in relationships is rarely literal fainting.
In relationships, it shows up as,

Sudden emotional flatness:

You were crying or raging, and then nothing.
Complete blankness.

Dissociative collapse:

You stop feeling like a person. You feel like you're watching from far away, or that you've ceased to exist.

Physical collapse:

Your legs give out, you need to sit or lie down, your body refuses to continue.

A sense of "I can't do this anymore":

Not as a thought, but as a full-body fact.

Withdrawal so total it feels like disappearance:

You don't just stop talking,
you stop being reachable.

The person on the receiving end may feel alarmed, confused, or helpless. They may not understand that what they're seeing is not manipulation. It is a system that has hit its absolute limit.

The Cost of Faint

Short-term:

Faint provides relief. The overload stops. The pain stops. The system gets a break, even if that break is a blackout.

Long-term:

Faint teaches the nervous system that disappearing is the only reliable escape.
Over time, the threshold for collapsing gets lower.
Small stressors begin to trigger shutdown.
The person loses confidence in their ability to stay present under pressure.
Relationships suffer because the other person can never predict when the collapse will come.

The deepest cost of Faint is this:
you stop trusting your own capacity to stay.
You begin to believe you are fragile, that you cannot handle things, that you will always eventually collapse.
And that belief becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy.

Why Faint Becomes a Default

For people with complex trauma, Faint can become the nervous system's last-resort response to anything that feels unsurvivable. The body learned, through repeated exposure to situations where fighting, running, freezing, and pleasing all failed, that shutting down is the only option left. So even when there's no real danger just a moment of intense relational overwhelm the Faint response floods in.

This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system that never got to learn that some threats are not actually threats.

How to Work With Faint

Notice the early signs.

The drop. The tunnel vision. The ringing ears. The sudden flatness. The urge to disappear completely. These are early warnings.

Ground physically — before the collapse.

Sit down. Put your head between your knees if needed. Feel your feet on the floor. Press your hands into something solid. Drink water. Cold water on the face or wrists can help reset the vagus nerve.

Name it.

"This is my Faint response. My system is overloaded. It's trying to protect me by shutting down. I am not dying. I am not disappearing. I am here."

Build capacity slowly.

Start with small stressors. Practice staying present for just a few seconds longer than feels comfortable. Use grounding techniques to stay in your body. Work with a trauma-informed therapist if the pattern is deep.
Faint is often the most entrenched response and the hardest to shift alone.

After the collapse, be gentle.

Don't shame yourself for shutting down. Rest. Recover. Your system just did something extreme to survive. When you're ready, reflect on what triggered it and what you might need next time.

Later, if possible, communicate the vulnerability underneath.

"I sometimes shut down when I feel completely overwhelmed. It's not about you. It's my nervous system. I'm working on it."

Communicate the truth, not the shame.

Instead of "Sorry I disappeared again," try "I shut down when I get overwhelmed. I'm learning to come back faster. Thank you for being patient with me."

posts.title: Flight
posts.body:
Flight is one of the two active defense responses in the defense cascade, alongside

Fight.

When the brain decides that a threat cannot be safely confronted, the body mobilizes into escape mode.
The goal is not to win.
The goal is to get away.
This is not a choice.
It is an automated survival program that activates when the nervous system judges that distance equals safety.

What Flight Feels Like Psychologically

The core psychological experience of Flight is urgency without direction.

A need to move, to leave, to get away

Restlessness, agitation, an inability to sit still

Racing thoughts that won't settle

Anxiety that feels like it's coming from everywhere and nowhere

A sense that if you just get far enough away, you'll be okay

The underlying emotion is not desire for freedom. It is fear of being caught. Caught by what? By the conversation. By the feeling. By the person who might get too close. By yourself.

Flight says: "If I leave before it reaches me, it can't hurt me."

Flight in Relationships

Flight does not always look like someone running out the door.
In relationships, it shows up as,

Avoiding difficult conversations:

"I don't want to talk about it right now." (Always "right now," never later.)

Filling the schedule:

Every moment booked, every silence avoided. If you're busy, you don't have to feel.

Emotional withdrawal:

You're physically present but mentally checked out. You answer questions without engaging.

Leaving before you're left:

Ending things preemptively so you don't have to experience rejection.

Distraction as a way of life:

Games, scrolling, porn, work, anything that keeps you from sitting still with yourself.

Running from intimacy:

When things get close, you get distant. When someone says "I love you," you panic.

The person on the receiving end feels abandoned. They may chase, which makes you run faster, which makes them chase harder. The cycle spirals.

The Cost of Flight

Short-term:

Flight protects you. It gets you out of the room. It buys you time. It keeps the feeling at arm's length. It works.

Long-term:

Flight keeps you from everything you say you want. You can't be loved if you don't stay. You can't be known if you're always halfway out the door. You can't build anything if you keep running from the building site. You can't feel the good stuff if you're running from the bad stuff.

The deepest cost of Flight is this: you become a stranger to your own life. You were there, but you weren't. You passed through, but you didn't stay.

Why Flight Becomes a Default

For people with complex trauma, Flight can become the nervous system's first response to anything. The body learned, through repeated exposure to situations where confronting the threat made it worse, that escape is the safest option. So even when there's no real danger,
just a difficult conversation, a moment of intimacy, a feeling that feels too big,
the Flight response floods in.

This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system that never got to learn that some threats are not actually threats.

How to Work With Flight

Notice the body signals.

Restless legs. Urge to stand up and walk away. Eyes scanning for exits. Shallow breath. Racing thoughts. These are early warnings.

Name it.

"This is my Flight response. It's trying to protect me. It's not the whole truth."

Pause.

Even three seconds. One breath. Create a gap before you bolt.

Ask what you're actually afraid of.

Not "what am I running from?" but "what am I afraid will happen if I stay?" The answer is usually: "I'll be trapped. I'll be hurt. I'll lose myself."

Stay one minute longer.

Not forever. Just one minute. Practice staying when your whole body says go. Let the discomfort peak and pass. Teach your nervous system that staying doesn't kill you.

Redirect the energy.

Flight energy is energy. It can go into running, walking, cleaning, or writing. Let the body complete the impulse without aiming it at a person or a relationship.

Later, if possible, communicate the vulnerability underneath.

"I need to leave because I'm scared, not because I don't care. I'm working on staying."

posts.title: Life-logging System
posts.body:
I've been working on something that sounds a bit obsessive.

a system that automatically records as much of my daily life as possible.

I mean everything that can be captured without me manually typing it in.

where I went, what I did on my computer, how I used my phone, how my body moved. The goal is to turn my life into structured data that I can actually learn from.

The Problem With Living by Memory
I don't trust my memory. Nobody should.

I'll finish a week and feel like I worked hard, but I couldn't tell you what I actually worked on.
I'll feel like I wasted too much time on my phone, but I won't know if it was 40 minutes or 4 hours. My sense of how I spend my time is vague, and vague impressions are easy to lie to myself about.

There's a name for the alternative, the Lyubishchev method, named after Alexander Lyubishchev, a Soviet biologist who tracked his time in 5-minute intervals for over 50 years. His principle was simple: record what you actually did, not what you planned to do. Start and end times. Duration. No judgment, just data. Then review at the end of the day, week, and month.

I've been trying to live by that principle, but doing it manually is exhausting. You forget to record. You round up. You skip days. The data becomes unreliable exactly when it would be most useful.

The system has three layers.

Collection

On my Windows laptop, ActivityWatch records window titles, browser URLs, and idle time. On my Android phone, Tasker captures screen unlocks and app switches, GPSLogger reports my location, and Gadgetbridge pulls step counts and heart rate from my smartwatch. All of this flows into a single event table, a long, flat table with columns like timestamp, domain, metric, value, and source.

Understanding

Every night at 11 PM, a script pulls the day's events, classifies them into time blocks (Work, Study, Life, Transport, Leisure, Health, Social, Other), and sends them to an AI model that writes a structured journal entry into my Obsidian vault.

Storage

Everything lives in a local SQLite database and an Obsidian vault with seven sections: Location, Phone, Time-Log, Tasks, Journal, AI-Sessions, and Reviews.

I didn't start from scratch.
I borrowed heavily from Felix Krause's FxLifeSheet,
an open-source project where he tracked over 100 metrics and 380,000 data points across three years. He manually answered more than 100 questions every day through a Telegram bot.

His conclusion after three years was honest:
the insights didn't justify the effort. He found a few genuinely useful patterns — his happiest moments were consistently after outdoor exercise, caffeine had almost no correlation with his productivity — but maintaining the system became a second job.

I think his mistake wasn't the tracking itself. It was that he had to do all the understanding manually. He recorded the data, then stared at 48 charts trying to find meaning. The AI layer I'm building is meant to solve exactly that problem.

I've also referenced ActivityWatch for passive desktop tracking, Dawarich for self-hosted location history, and Gadgetbridge for pulling wearable data without going through a vendor's cloud.

If I visualize my data clearly enough, can I actually change my behavior?

Not in a vague "be more mindful" way.
I mean concretely.
If I can see that I spend 11 hours a week in a specific app that I don't even enjoy, can I reclaim that time?
If I can see that my mood consistently drops on days I skip exercise, can I use that as leverage to actually exercise?

The Lyubishchev method is built on the assumption that seeing the truth changes what you do. I'm not sure that's always true, there's a gap between knowing and acting.
But I want to find out for myself, with my own data, rather than accepting either the productivity-guru version ("track everything!") or the cynical version ("none of this matters").

AI involves

The most interesting part of this project is the AI layer, not because it's flashy, but because it solves the one problem that made Felix's system unsustainable.

His data was rich but flat. He knew he slept 7 hours. He knew he drank 2 cups of coffee. What he couldn't easily capture was why he felt a certain way, or what he was thinking during a specific block of time. Those things are hard to reduce to a number.

AI can help close that gap. Instead of asking myself 100 fixed questions every night, I can have the system read my day's events first, notice where the data is thin or strange, and ask me only the 3 or 4 questions that actually matter:

"You had no screen activity between 2 and 4 PM but your location shows you were at the office. What were you doing?"

"This is the third day in a row your caffeine intake was above average and your sleep was under 6 hours. Is something going on?"

That's a fundamentally different relationship with self-tracking.
It's not a form to fill out. It's a conversation - one where the AI already knows most of the answers and just needs you to fill in the gaps that only you can.

Next step

I'm still early.
I've only run the full pipeline once, and the first journal entry it produced was mostly wrong, the AI had to invent a timeline because the rule engine dropped 82% of the day's data. That's now fixed, with regression tests.

The next step is to let it run for a full week, then look at the output honestly and ask, is this actually useful?
If it is, I'll add more sources, phone notifications, spending data, maybe voice memos.
If it isn't, I'll cut what doesn't matter.

Felix spent three years and concluded it wasn't worth it.
I'm hoping the AI layer changes that equation. But I won't know until I run it long enough to see my own patterns, and that's the only honest way to find out.

The project is built on top of FxLifeSheet (MIT licensed) and uses ActivityWatch, Dawarich, Gadgetbridge, Tailscale, and DeepSeek.
