posts.title: Freeze
posts.body:
Freeze is the third defense response in the defense cascade.

When the brain decides that neither fight nor flight is possible, the body mobilizes into shutdown mode.
This is not a choice.
It is an automated survival program that activates when the threat is too close, too fast, too overwhelming.
It is what happens when there is no way out.

What Freeze Feels Like Psychologically

The core psychological experience of Freeze is a sudden absence of self.

Going blank. Thoughts stop. Words disappear.

Feeling frozen in place. The body won't move, even though part of you wants to.

Dissociation. You feel like you're watching yourself from a distance.

Numbness. Emotions that were just there are suddenly unreachable.

Time distortion. Seconds feel like minutes. Or everything slows down.

A sense of unreality. The room feels fake. Other people feel like actors.

The underlying state is not calm. It is overwhelm so complete that the system shuts down to survive it.

Freeze says: "If I don't move, maybe it won't hurt me. If I disappear, maybe I'll still be here when it's over."

Freeze in Relationships

Freeze does not always look like trauma.
In relationships, it shows up as,

Going silent during conflict:

Not because you're punishing the other person, but because your brain literally cannot produce words.

Being unable to respond:

They say something. You know you should say something. Nothing comes out.

Dissociating during intimacy:

You're physically present, but mentally you're somewhere else entirely.

Forgetting conversations:

Not because you don't care, but because your brain didn't record them.

Feeling "blank" when asked what you think or feel:

You genuinely don't know. The information isn't accessible.

The person on the receiving end feels shut out. They may interpret your silence as rejection or indifference. They don't realize that your silence is not a message — it is a survival state.

The Cost of Freeze

Short-term:

Freeze protects you. When nothing else works, it shuts down the pain. It keeps you from fighting a fight you can't win. It keeps you from running when there's nowhere to go.

Long-term:

Freeze disconnects you from your own life. You lose access to your own feelings. You lose access to your own body. You lose relationships. You lose time. You become a stranger to yourself.

Why Freeze Becomes a Default

For people with complex trauma, Freeze can become the nervous system's response to anything. The body learned, through repeated exposure to situations where fighting back made it worse and running away was not possible, that shutdown is the safest option. So even when there's no real danger, just a raised voice, a sudden demand, a moment of conflict, the Freeze response floods in.

This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system that never got to learn that some threats are not actually threats.

How to Work With Freeze

Notice the body signals.

You're not speaking, but not by choice. You feel far away. The room feels fake. You can't feel your body. These are early warnings.

Name it.

"This is my Freeze response. It's trying to protect me. It's not the whole truth."

Ground yourself physically.

Feel your feet on the floor. Press your hands against the wall. Hold something cold or textured. Move your body, wiggle your toes, stretch your fingers, roll your shoulders. Movement is the antidote to Freeze.

Slow your breath.

Exhale longer than you inhale. Let the belly soften. Tell the nervous system: "We're not trapped anymore."

Give yourself time.

You cannot force yourself out of Freeze. You can only create the conditions, safety, movement, breath and let it happen.

Later, if possible, communicate the vulnerability underneath.

"When I go quiet, it's not because I don't care. My system shuts down. I'm working on it."

posts.title: Fawn
posts.body:
Fawn is one of the hidden defense responses in the defense cascade.

When the brain decides a threat cannot be fought, cannot be fled, and cannot be frozen through, the body mobilizes into appeasement mode.
This is not a choice.
It is an automated survival program that activates before conscious thought catches up.
It is what a child does when there is no escape.

What Fawn Feels Like Psychologically

The core psychological experience of Fawn is a compulsive need to keep the other person okay, so that you can be okay.

A constant low-grade anxiety about whether the other person is upset

An urge to apologize, explain, or fix things before anyone asks

Difficulty identifying what you want, because you're so tuned into what they want

A sense of relief when they seem satisfied, and dread when they seem displeased

Anger that you suppress immediately, because anger might break the peace

The underlying emotion is not love. Love is the surface. Underneath is fear of conflict, fear of abandonment, fear of being seen as difficult or selfish.

Fawn says: "If I keep you happy, you won't leave me."

Fawn in Relationships

Fawn does not always look like weakness.
In relationships, it shows up as,

Over-apologizing:

"Sorry" becomes a reflex, even when you did nothing wrong.

Over-explaining:

You write paragraphs to justify a simple preference, afraid of being misunderstood.

Compulsive caregiving:

You anticipate their needs, sometimes before they know them, because their comfort feels like your responsibility.

No boundaries:

You say yes when you mean no. You swallow your needs to keep the peace.

Conflict avoidance:

Any disagreement feels like a threat. You concede immediately, even when you disagree.

Resentment buildup:

You give and give, then feel invisible and unappreciated — but you never say it, because saying it might cause conflict.

Loss of self:

Over time, you don't know what you actually want anymore. You only know what they want.

The person on the receiving end may feel loved, or they may feel suffocated. Either way, they are not connecting with you. They are connecting with the version of you that exists to serve them.

The Cost of Fawn

Short-term:

Fawn keeps the peace. It prevents conflict. It makes you feel needed. It gives you a temporary sense of safety.

Long-term:

Fawn destroys you. You disappear. You attract takers. You accumulate resentment. You cannot be truly loved. Your body breaks down.

Why Fawn Becomes a Default

For people with complex trauma, Fawn can become the nervous system's first response to anything. The body learned, through repeated exposure to environments where expressing needs was ignored or punished, that appeasement is the safest option. So even when there's no real danger—just a slightly cold tone, a delayed reply, a hint of displeasure—the Fawn response floods in.

This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system that never got to learn that some threats are not actually threats.

How to Work With Fawn

Notice the body signals.

Are you smiling right now? Do you actually feel like smiling? Are you about to say "sorry"? Did you actually do something wrong? Are you saying yes? Do you actually want to? These are early warnings.

Name it.

"This is my Fawn response. It's trying to protect me. It's not the whole truth."

Pause.

Even three seconds. One breath. Create a gap before you agree to anything.

Ask what you actually need.

Not "what do they want to hear?" but "what do I actually want right now? What do I actually need to feel safe?"

Practice saying no.

Start small. Skip the gathering you don't want to attend. Don't reply to the message you don't want to reply to. Say "I can't do that" without following it with a paragraph of explanation.

Let people be disappointed.

You cannot keep everyone happy. You were never supposed to. Someone being disappointed in you does not mean you are bad. It means you are a person with boundaries.

Later, if possible, communicate the vulnerability underneath.

"I said yes because I was afraid you'd be upset. I'm trying to unlearn that. I care about you. That's the truth."

Communicate the truth, not the appeasement.

Instead of "Whatever you want!" try "I'd prefer this, but I'm open to hearing what you think."
Instead of "Sorry I'm such a mess," try "I'm having a hard day. I'm glad you're here."

posts.title: Fight
posts.body:
When the Body Chooses to Confront

Fight is one of the two active defense responses in the defense cascade.

When the brain decides a threat can be confronted and control can be reclaimed, the body mobilizes into attack mode.
This is not a choice.
It is an automated survival program that activates before conscious thought catches up.

What Fight Feels Like Psychologically

The core psychological experience of Fight is a surge of aggressive energy aimed at reclaiming control.

Anger, irritation, or rage rising fast

A need to confront, to demand answers, to push back

Urgency, intensity

a narrowing of focus onto the threat

The underlying emotion is not really anger. Anger is the surface. Underneath is fear of being powerless, fear of being taken advantage of, fear of being dismissed or erased.

Fight says: "If I don't attack first, I will be hurt."

Fight in Relationships

Fight does not always look like physical aggression.
In relationships, it shows up as,

Interrogation :

"Why haven't you replied? What were you doing? Who were you with?"

Accusation:

"You don't care about me. You never did."

Control:

Needing to know everything, needing to define the terms, needing the other person to submit to your version of reality.

Verbal attack:

Sarcasm, criticism, bringing up old wounds to win the argument.

Emotional explosion:

Sudden bursts of anger that feel disproportionate to the trigger.

The person on the receiving end feels attacked. They may retreat, freeze, or fawn. The Fight response, in trying to protect you, pushes the other person away.

The Cost of Fight

Short-term:

Fight gives you a sense of power. You feel like you're doing something. You're not helpless.

Long-term:

Fight damages connection. It makes people afraid of you. It makes you afraid of yourself. And it exhausts your body.

Why Fight Becomes a Default

For people with complex trauma, Fight can become the nervous system's first response to anything. The body learned, through repeated exposure to threat, that attack is the safest option. So even when there's no real danger—just an ambiguous text, a delayed reply, a slightly cold tone—the Fight response floods in.

This is not a character flaw. It is a nervous system that never got to learn that some threats are not actually threats.

How to Work With Fight

Notice the body signals.

Clenched jaw. Tight fists. Shallow breath. Heat in the chest. These are early warnings.

Name it.

"This is my Fight response. It's trying to protect me. It's not the whole truth."

Pause.

Even three seconds. One breath. Create a gap.

Ask what you actually need.

Not "what do I want to say?" but "what am I afraid of right now? What do I actually need to feel safe?"

Redirect the energy.

Fight energy is energy. It can go into running, writing, cleaning, or simply shaking it out. Let the body complete the impulse without aiming it at a person.

Later, if possible, communicate the vulnerability underneath.

"I got angry because I was scared. I was scared because I care. That's the truth."

posts.title: Shadow
posts.body:
I don't think they ever hurt me.
And I will not punish myself because I took those chances, or for being too sincere, too real.

Life is just as fragile as a bubble.
They have left a mark.
WE ALL LEFT A MARK.
I carry these things. I carry these people.
I know I could lose myself in the blankness of paper again,
but I will never let them go.
They have lived inside my soul.

Oh, hope! The false hope!
The dim, melancholy soul of mine,
When will it be shined?

A door was opened.
Twilight streamed through the chink,
Projecting the shadow of my mind.

posts.title: S & N
posts.body:
S & N

Jungian Cognitive Functions

The root of all human suffering, ultimately, comes down to communication.
But the greatest tragedy in communication isn't a language barrier.
It's something deeper,
an absolute incompatibility of underlying operating systems.

Jungian typology (the foundation of MBTI)
People fall into two categories,
outward, inward. This isn't just a difference in personality. It's two entirely different operating systems.

The Chasm Between S and N

In Jung's eight cognitive functions, there are two core perceiving functions: S (Sensing) and N (Intuition).
They are two fundamental ways humans gather information, and the source of humanity's deepest divisions.

S (Sensing): Grounded in reality and experience.
They trust what they can see, what they've lived through, and the order that has been proven by the past.

N (Intuition): Grounded in possibility and meaning. They trust abstract logic, future metaphors, and the invisible world of the spirit.

Beneath these, there is a further split between "Introverted" and "Extraverted." Among these, the opposition between
Si (Introverted Sensing) and Ni (Introverted Intuition) represents humanity's most extreme pair of underlying logics which is Pragmatism and Idealism.

Si: Pragmatism — The External World of "Tangibility"

People dominated by Si (Introverted Sensing)
see the world through the lens of Pragmatism.

Core logic: The past is truth. To live is to maintain established order and secure physical safety.

The world in their eyes: Made of things that can be seen, touched, and measured—matter, rules, daily routines. Eating is for sustenance. Studying is for a job. Marriage is for reproduction.

When they look at people: They see physical body, actions, practical value. If you tell them about your pain, your soul, or your abyss, they don't see "depth." They see "unpredictable trouble."

Their love often looks like: "coming home on time," "bringing you food," "solving practical problems." They cannot understand why you care about a cloud, a poem, or a feeling.

Ni: Idealism — The Internal World of the "Spirit"

People dominated by Ni (Introverted Intuition)
see the world through the lens of Idealism.

Core logic: The future is truth. To live is to search for meaning, excavate essence, and achieve spiritual transcendence.

The world in their eyes: Made of metaphors, symbols, deep patterns, and emotional resonance. Eating is for experiencing life. Studying is for understanding truth. Love is for the soul's redemption.

When they look at people: they see shell, vessel, shallow routines, feel they are imprisoned in a cage of reality, unable to touch true spiritual freedom.

This is why you cannot talk pragmatism to an idealist, nor idealism to a pragmatist.

Because your Protocols are entirely different, even mutually exclusive:

(Ni) send signals using the Idealism Protocol,
soul, meaning, depth, sacrifice, breakthrough.

(Si) receive signals using the Pragmatism Protocol,
pressure, heaviness, control, impracticality, danger,
from Ni.

Neither of you is wrong.
The mistake is trying to forcibly connect to another world using your own protocol.

This world is cruel.

Pragmatists are forever looking for a comrade to face reality with.

Idealists are forever looking for a soul to face loneliness with.

If you are an idealist, please do not try to reform a pragmatist. Do not try to pull them out of the soil of reality and throw them into your deep sea. You will only suffocate them and shatter yourself.
The only thing you can do is find another idealist, or learn to draw an absolutely safe boundary for yourself between reality and idealism.
Vice versa.

Learn it, understand it, accept it

posts.title: Mirage
posts.body:
I don't know what the fuck I did.

I met him

I started sending him long messages.
Confessing feelings that were too heavy for two weeks.
I wrote poems at 2 a.m.
I told him things I’d never told anyone.
Every reply from him felt like a sign from the universe.
I thought if I was just honest enough, vulnerable enough, he would finally see me.

But he was the avoidant one. The more I reached out, the more he pulled back.
No explanation. No goodbye. Just silence.

That's the anxious-avoidant trap. I wanted closeness. He wanted space.
Neither of us was evil.
We were just two wounded people acting out old patterns that never fit.

I had built a statue of him in my mind. A perfect figure made of my own hopes, my own fantasies, my desperate need for someone to complete me.
I worshipped it.
I wrote poems to it.
I wept at its feet.
But it was made of projections.
It had no foundation in reality.
It cracked.

Never a god. Just a fearful, limited, avoidant human.
He couldn't save me. He couldn't complete me.

Running away from the shadow.

I built a temple around a mirage.

I had two choices.
Glue it back together and chase the illusion in every new face.
Or realize that the only thing that was ever real was the part of me that did the worshipping.
The longing.
The depth.
The capacity to love that deeply.

I picked up the pieces, to build something else.
Something that can not be revealed.

I am still learning. Learning. Learning.
To be stupid. To be stupid.

posts.title: Individuation
posts.body:
Individuation, put simply, is the process of a person finally becoming themselves.

Not becoming a better person, not becoming a more perfect person, but becoming the real, whole self.

Jung said, the most important task in one's life is not to please the world, not to play the roles others expect, but to gather back the scattered, repressed, and denied parts of oneself, piece by piece, and reassemble them into a whole.

My understanding of individuation has three layers.

The first layer is admitting that you contain contradictions.

I am not only someone who wants to be loved.
I am also someone who is afraid of getting close.
I am not only a deeply affectionate person.
I am also someone with arrogance, with shadow, with aggression.
I used to want to hide the ugly parts and keep only the clean side.

But the first step of individuation is admitting they all exist.

I am not a purely good person.

People are complex. Very complex.

What am I? Someone complex beyond complexity.

The second layer is taking back your projections.

We all fall in love with our own projections.

When we look at a person, we never see them as they truly are.
We see the shadow of our own inner world.
People who lack love look for a mother's warmth in someone else.
People who are anxious look for certainty in someone else.
People who love writing poetry look for the echo of resonance in someone else.
Everyone is searching, but what they are searching for is always the missing piece inside themselves.

But the biggest problem with projection is that it is never real.
You are not in love with that person. You are in love with the version you imagined in your head.
You put them into a script you built, giving them the shape you wanted them to have.
The moment they deviate even slightly, you get hurt.

Because they don't fit your script, you feel they betrayed your love.
But from beginning to end, they never agreed to play that role.

If a person doesn't fill their own gaps, they will repeat the same thing forever. Change the person, change the face, the story stays the same. Because that person is not the answer, just the carrier of your projection. You put your love on them, but that love was never theirs. It belonged to the empty place inside you.

Real love begins the moment you take the projection back. You no longer ask the other person to fill you. You no longer treat them as your cure. You just look at them, a real person with flaws, limitations, and their own rhythm.
You stop loving your imagination. You start learning to love them as they are.

The third layer is accepting yourself, and your past.

The trauma, the heaviness, the silence, the awkwardness, the overexertion, all the foolish things you did and all the nights you fell apart.

They are not stains I need to erase. They are the necessary path that made me who I am.

Individuation is not a destination.
It is not something you suddenly achieve one day and then remain stable forever.
It is an ongoing process. You keep knowing yourself, keep integrating new fragments, keep moving forward.

My understanding now is that individuation is not about becoming a person without wounds, but about becoming a person who can live fully, even with the wounds.

posts.title: Antithesis
posts.body:
When you see a person,
Which part do you look at first?
The vessel that carries the soul,
Or the soul that can exist anywhere, forever.

This internal, melancholy soul of mine,
Blooming in the dim twilight,
Seen through the surface of your body.

Soul purged by fire.
Amber falls—nourishing the field that stands.

Then everything,
Judged by the foul one.
The other side of the moon.
Where it begins, where it ends.

posts.title: Observer - Fragment IV
posts.body:
I do not feel. I do not judge. I do not act. I watch.

I am the one who sits in the back of the skull, silent, taking notes while the others burn.

When the romanticist drowns in a single glance, I record the temperature of the water.

When the idealist wants to tear the world down, I write down what he says.

When the advocate reaches for someone too fast, I am the one who notes the exact moment his hand began to shake.

I am not cold. I am simply unwilling to lie to myself.

I have been mistaken for cruelty.
I have been mistaken for arrogance.
But I was never here to punish.
I was here to keep the whole thing from collapsing.
When the heart is screaming and the mind is on fire, someone has to stay sober.
That someone is me.

I do not stop the pain.
I just make sure it doesn't kill the body that carries it.

I see everything.
The contradictions.
The patterns.
The moments when one part of me is pretending to be another. I see how the romanticist dresses up his hunger as poetry.
I see how the idealist uses his standards to avoid vulnerability.
I see how the advocate sometimes acts not out of courage, but out of fear of regret.

I do not intervene.
I observe.

I am a mirror.
I am reflection itself.
I am the witness.
I am the silence behind every word. And without me, none of the rest would survive themselves.

posts.title: The Fire and The Trap
posts.body:
I have been cold for so long that warmth feels like a threat.

When you spend years in the cold, you learn things. You learn to keep your hands in your pockets. You learn to walk fast so you don't feel the wind. You learn to stop expecting anyone to come with a blanket. You build a life around the absence of heat—and after a while, you almost stop noticing it's missing.

Then a small fire appears.

It's nothing dramatic. Just a flicker. A tiny spark of warmth in the distance. And here's the strange thing: instead of moving toward it, you flinch.

Not because you don't want warmth. You want it more than anything. But because you've been burned before. Because every time you reached for something warm in the past, it turned out to be a trick. A test. A door that opened just long enough for you

to walk through, then slammed shut behind you.

So your first instinct isn't gratitude. It's suspicion.

Is this real?
Is this a trap?
Am I seeing something that isn't there?

You start interrogating the fire. You circle it. You poke it. You look for evidence that it's fake. You tell yourself you're just being careful. You're just protecting yourself.

But that's not protection. That's the cold, talking.

The cold doesn't want to be healed. The cold wants to be right. It wants you to stay in the darkness where it's safe. Where you can't be rejected, because you never asked for anything in the first place. Where you can't be disappointed, because you never believed in anything.

The cold is a liar dressed up as wisdom.

I don't have a clean ending for this. I don't have a solution. I'm not going to pretend I've suddenly learned to trust the fire, or that the fear is gone.

But I'm starting to notice something.

The fire isn't the trap.

The trap is believing that warmth is always a trick, that kindness always comes with a price, that anyone who reaches for you must be trying to hurt you.

The trap is staying frozen so long that you stop being able to recognize love when it arrives.

So I'm trying something new. I'm not running into the fire. I'm not diving headfirst into something I can't see. But I'm not backing away either.

I'm standing close enough to feel the heat.

I'm letting it be what it is. Small. Real. Uncertain.

I'm not asking it to keep me warm forever. I'm just letting myself be warm for now.

That's enough. That's more than I've ever allowed myself before.

posts.title: Romanticist - Fragment I
posts.body:
I feel before I understand.
That is the burden and the gift of being it.

I do not experience life in muted tones.
Everything arrives at full volume.
A glance lingers longer than it should.
A silence carries more weight than any sentence.
I am drawn to the ache of things, the unspoken, the unfinished, the almost.

I am naive,
I romanticize,
the surface of the world may is too thin for me.
I need to find meaning underneath it, or I cannot breathe.

I do not choose intensity.
It chooses me.
It floods me.
It makes me write things at midnight that I cannot say in daylight.
It makes me fall for the possibility of someone before I have even met them.

I am weak.
I am permanently exposed.
I walk through the world without skin.

posts.title: Advocate - Fragment III
posts.body:
I act.
Am I fearless?
No? I am afraid not. I am terrified.
I cannot stand the alternative.

The advocate is what happens when the romanticist and the idealist finally agree.
This matters, and it is worth the risk.
The advocate is the hand that reaches out.
The voice that says the thing.
The body that steps forward when every other part of me wants to retreat.

But the advocate pays the price.
He is the one who lives with the consequences.
He sends the message that cannot be unsent.
He speaks the truth that cannot be taken back.
He is the one who waits in silence after, wondering if he has ruined everything.

I can not always win. But I will never disappear.
I am not just a person who feels and thinks.
I am a person who moves.
Even when it hurts.
Even when it's terrifying.
Even when no one responds.

The advocate is the only version of me that gets to exist in the real world.
The romanticist and the idealist are internal.
The advocate is the one who walks out the door.

He is the most vulnerable of the three.
He is the most painful one.
He can not take the burden of this misery.
Cry, sometimes.
But that makes him the most alive one.

posts.title: Idealist - Fragment II
posts.body:
I am in a constant state of disappointment, because I live with a blueprint of how things should be.

I believe in purity.
I believe in depth.
I believe that connection should be sacred and that people should mean what they say. I
believe in a version of the world that does not exist.
And because it does not exist,
I am forever grieving something I have never actually had.

I am not arrogant.
I am heartbroken.
I look at the world and see everything that is missing.
I look at myself and see everything I have not yet become.
I hold everyone, including me,
to an impossible standard, and then suffers when we fall short.

It isolates me.
It makes me feel like a stranger in every room.
But it also protects you.
Because if you refuse to accept less than what you believe in, you will never settle for a life that is hollow.

posts.title: Urge
posts.body:
The urge, the urge of what?
Dissecting yourself, a decomposed corpse.
Every bit of you, inside you,
Pointing in the same direction.
The one that most would ignore.
The soul. The fissures in the soul.
What is it? What happened?
A sharp, painful observation.
The contemporary world, a morgue.
Disgruntled, apathetic pedestrians.
Connected, seemingly, but lost.
Lost in those sounds, the interpretations.
Isolation, the lowered head.
As if it were the execution. Beheading.
What is it?
Disappointment. A symbol.
A symbol of not following the trend.
A symbol of searching for beauty in this misery.
What happened?
Too much, too heavy. But small and real.

posts.title: Spinning
posts.body:
When I lie on my bed,
I feel the world is spinning,
A black hole,
Trying to drag me into an endless loop,
Where it is hard to believe that you exist.
You, controlled by a distant being.

Everything is drifting away from you.
You project a perfect saying,
While clawing at concrete walls,
Burying your feelings.
Sounds start fading.
You were listening.

Yet morning dew stirs the sea.
The smallest thing at dawn,
And everything begins to move.

posts.title: Contradiction
posts.body:
A walking contradiction, torn to pieces between what you feel and what you know.
Hanging around as you always, back and forth,
holding a book that no one can understand,
showing people that you do not trend.

Echoes shatter. The obscure book in your hand, becomes lines of poetry drifting on the breeze.
The verses, carried by the wind, stumble in the air where it meant,
scattered into pieces where the ground has been nourished by the flood.
Full of blood. Burdens that you carry.

Cold wires into your head, strangling your death.
An apocalyptic body becomes other people's heaven,
a lie that was never exposed to the sunlight.
Fragments of your cold body consumed by foul creatures; heaven falls.

Then you realize you were the light,
a beam of light that only shone in reverse.

posts.title: Indecision
posts.body:
I kept every hesitation folded like a secret prayer
warm, unlit, trembling,
and let the silence hold what my lips never dared to bless you with.

Perhaps just a gentle whim of touch to you.
You breezed past every room in my chest.

Those unspoken sentences incarnate in an invisible hand
Struggled to grip something in the air.
As I was trying to follow your steps.

I ran amok. In indecision.
Hanging onto the edge in my rear view.
My existence turning into intangible feelings.
Floating in the atmosphere where every word that never reached you

breathes, quietly, waits, from a room you already left.

posts.cardTitle: TELL ME, WHAT IS THE VOICE INSIDE ME
posts.title: Tell Me, What Is the Voice Inside Me
posts.body:
Tell me, what is the voice inside me.
What it has been trying to say.
Saying to me. Letting me know.

Scar tissues integrated to a rearranged heart.
The frail flutter of a dying beat.

My body, my vessel no longer treat.

Overture. Intermission. Epilogue.

It never ends.

A reel without ending. So desperately.
To reach the end.

Nothing there. But emptiness.
A colossus of blood and sinew.

Should I go? Is it real?
To love in a void.

A lament wrung from agony.
Echoes lingered around your ears.

Disappearing. Fading.

Exacerbating. Tormenting.

The darkhole you put yourself in, where it leads.
A hand, reached you, missed again. On a train, it stopped.
A platform, where you met.
Yesterday does not answer when you call.
The river does not run backward.
The wound does not forget.

Prayed, were you sincere enough, did anyone answer.
I believe it did.

Where you met.
And you gripped.

posts.title: Small
posts.body:
It worked, for a while. I became easier to love, quieter, safer, less.

People stayed longer. They didn’t flinch when I spoke, because I wasn’t really speaking. I was performing. I was giving them a version of me that was easier to digest.

But every night, I felt like I was disappearing.

Because the version of me they liked wasn’t me. It was a costume. A mask I had worn so well that even I started to forget what was underneath.

You can’t be loved for who you are if you never show anyone who you are.

You can be liked. You can be tolerated. You can be invited to things. But you can’t be loved. Not really. Not in the way that matters.

Because love requires being seen. And if you’re hiding, the only thing anyone can love is the hiding.

So I stopped.

Not all at once. It was slow. Painful. I lost people. Some of them left because I became 'too much' again. Some of them drifted away because they only ever liked the smaller version of me. And that hurt. It still hurts, sometimes.

I’m still learning. I still catch myself shrinking sometimes, pulling back a thought, softening a truth, making myself easier. But I’m catching it faster now. And every time I catch it, I choose differently.

I choose to be heavy. To take up space. To say the thing that scares me. To be too much, if that’s what it takes.

Because I would rather be alone as myself than surrounded as someone else.

And maybe, one day, someone will look at all of it, the weight, the intensity, the honesty, the strange, and not look away. Maybe they’ll stay.

But even if no one does, at least I’ll know that what they see is real.

And that has to be enough.

posts.title: Heavy
posts.body:
I am someone who feels everything deeply and says it out loud, even when it terrifies me.

I don’t do small talk. I don’t do surface-level. I don’t do “how are you” and “fine, thanks.” I want to know what’s underneath. I want to know what hurts, what matters, what keeps you up at night. I want the real thing, or nothing at all.

I’ve been told I’m too much. Too intense. Too direct. A bit strange. And for a long time, I believed that. I tried to shrink myself, to soften my edges, to be someone easier to be around.

But I couldn’t do it. It felt like betraying who I actually am and the thing I have, my honesty.

posts.cardTitle: WHO I AM WHEN NO ONE IS WATCHING - I CAN'T HOLD SOMEONE'S TRUST AND NOT GIVE IT BACK
posts.title: Who I Am When No One Is Watching - I Can't Hold Someone's Trust And Not Give It Back
posts.body:
Something happened on the subway today.

A woman sat next to me. The train stopped. She didn't realize it was her stop until the last second. When she did, she panicked, rushed out of the carriage, and the doors closed behind her.

She left her bag on the seat.

I heard her yelling from the platform. She had realized, too late, that she'd forgotten it.

I stood up immediately. I grabbed the bag. I got off at the next stop, crossed over, and took a train going back.

I didn't know if she understood what I was trying to say through the glass. I didn't know if she'd still be there when I got back. But I went anyway.

Because once you're holding something that belongs to someone else—once you've picked up that weight—you can't just put it down and walk away. You carry a responsibility. You carry their trust. And I can't carry someone's trust and not give it back.

That's just who I am.

I found her. I gave her the bag. She thanked me in a way that didn't need many words. It was ineffable—something you feel but can't quite say.

And here's what I've been thinking since:

Most people would have handed the bag to a station worker and moved on. They'd have told themselves they did their part. They'd have absolved themselves.

And I don't say that to judge them. I say it because I know what it feels like to be the odd one out. The one who runs back. The one who cares too much about a stranger's bag. The one who carries things other people have learned to put down.

Sometimes that makes me feel vulnerable.

Because in a world that's mostly indifferent, caring this much can feel like a weakness. Like you're the only one still holding onto something the rest of the world has let go of.

But I've come to believe that's not weakness. That's just being awake.

And here's something I've realized: every single thing we do leaves a mark. Every word, every action. You can't escape it. You can either hurt someone or help someone—but you can't do nothing. Even indifference is a kind of action.

I don't do what I do for a reward. I don't do it so someone will call me a good person. I do it because I know how much a single moment can matter. A small act of care can change someone's entire day. And a small act of coldness can break someone for weeks.

We carry more power than we think. Our words and actions can make the world a little warmer, or a little colder. We choose, every time, which one it's going to be.

I don't know if she'll remember me. She probably won't. But I'll remember her. I'll remember the way she looked when I handed her the bag back—relieved, grateful, and a little bit stunned that a stranger would go out of his way like that.

That moment was worth it. Not because it made me feel important—but because it reminded me of who I am, and what I'm capable of putting into the world.

I run back for people. That's just me.

And even if the world doesn't always understand that, I'm not going to stop.

Because your words and your actions can affect others. You can make the world a better place, or a worse one. And I know which one I'm choosing.

posts.cardTitle: I SENTENCED MYSELF FOR TWO YEARS
posts.title: I Sentenced Myself for Two Years
posts.body:
I put myself on trial.

I trained every day on the track team. Pushed myself harder than I should have.
But I was also completely isolated—cold, arrogant, telling myself I didn't need anyone.

My logic was simple: Work hard enough, and you win. But deeper down, I had another belief: If I suffer enough, someone will finally see me. The pain will be worth it because it will earn me recognition.

Then I went to my first real competition. One guy lapped me. Just ran right past like I wasn't there.

And I realized something that broke me: Working hard and winning? There's no actual connection. And suffering and being seen? There's no guarantee either.

I called it "self-probation." Like I was on trial, trying to prove I was good enough. And the verdict came back: not good enough.

I sat with that for a long time.

Eventually, I figured out the lie: Success isn't the only reason to work hard. And pain doesn't guarantee a reward.

If you only do it to win, you break when you lose. If you only do it to be seen, you break when nobody's watching.

But if you do it because it's who you are—then nobody can take that from you.

So if you're giving everything and getting nothing back—hear this:

You don't have to prove your worth. You don't have to suffer just to matter.

The work itself can be the reward. If you let it.

The race isn't about winning. It's about not stopping.

posts.cardTitle: IN THE MIDDLE OF THE WORLD
posts.title: In the Middle of the World
posts.body:
I watched Moonlight on a laptop at eight in the morning. It is a film about skin and water and light, and my screen made all of it smaller. It still got through.I am still thinking about a boy floating in the sea with a grown man's hand under his back.

Juan is a drug dealer. He is also the only adult in the film who asks Chiron a real question and then waits for the answer. He teaches him to swim, tells him that in moonlight black boys look blue, and a few scenes later you find out he sells to Chiron's mother. The film does not balance those two facts or explain them away. It lets them sit in the same body, the way they do in actual people.

In moonlight, black boys look blue.

Three names

Little, Chiron, Black. The chapter titles give the whole thing away before it starts. The first is what the neighbourhood calls him, the second is what his mother shouts when she is not really shouting at him, the third is what he builds after deciding that soft is not survivable. By the last chapter he is wearing gold and driving with the windows down, and it mostly looks like a costume he never got around to taking off.

What got me was how little anybody says. His mother loves him and cannot say it without screaming. Kevin cannot say it at all until twenty minutes before the end. Chiron spends most of three chapters looking at the ground. Everything is shot blue, and somewhere around the beach scene the blue stops being a colour and turns into the temperature of the room.

The diner

At the end Kevin cooks him a meal, and Chiron says: you're the only man who's ever touched me. Then he says it happened in the middle of the world. It is not a good sentence. He says it badly, with a pause in the wrong place, and that is the part I keep replaying, because it is how the true things come out when you have spent a whole life not saying them.

I have been trying to say the important things sooner than I am comfortable with. That goes against most of what I taught myself about keeping a straight face. Watching a man mumble the truest sentence of his life into a plate of food made me want to be less impressive and more honest.

Two hours of people not saying it, then one minute of someone saying it. That is the whole film, and it is enough.

posts.title: Before Heading Out
posts.body:
A year. That's how long I've been away from school. People kept asking when I'd go back, like it was only about a date. It wasn't — it was about whether the version of me that left could still fit into the desk I left behind.

What school never taught me

A year away will teach you more than four years in. Some lessons only land when you're alone with them — no syllabus, no grade. Nobody teaches you how to sit with yourself when the noise stops, what to do at 3 a.m. when you're the only one awake in your own head. The hardest classes aren't the ones you register for — they're the ones life enrolls you in, and there's no dropping them.

The things that change you the most are the things no one thought to warn you about.

Loneliness

It's not the movie version — no rain on the window. It's quieter: eating alone because everyone's busy, not wanting to ask because you don't want to be the one who always asks. Having things to say and no one to interrupt. The long stretch of evening that should've been shared.

And here's something I'm not embarrassed to say out loud: I want a girlfriend. Not as a fix — I learned that the hard way. Someone to be quiet with. Someone to be known by. I spent a long time pretending wanting closeness was a weakness. It's not. But the loneliness taught me I had to learn to be okay alone first — otherwise you don't find a person, you find a place to put the empty.

The mind, and how to keep it

This is the part nobody warned me about either — how thin the line gets between "I'm fine" and "I'm not." How a bad month quietly becomes a bad year. I didn't know I was carrying psychological weight until it started leaking into everything: sleep, appetite, the way I answered my own name. The mind doesn't announce its problems — it normalizes them, until "off" feels like your baseline.

What helped wasn't dramatic. Sleep. Sunlight. Honest conversations with people who don't flinch. Knowing the difference between a bad day and a bad season, and the nerve to ask for help when it's the second one. Therapy isn't weakness. Medication isn't failure. Saying "I'm not okay" is the first chapter of getting okay.

You can't think your way out of a mind that's unwell. Sometimes you have to let other people hold the flashlight.

Before heading out

So this is the last update before I go back. I'm bringing the year with me — the loneliness, the wanting, the bad weeks, the slow climb back. The things nobody taught me and nobody warned me about. They're the only curriculum that ever stuck.

Be brave. Be genuine. Be humble. Take care of your mind — it's the only one you get. And don't be a dick, especially not to yourself.

posts.title: Don't Be a Dick
posts.body:
We were playing basketball. 5 on 5 full-court basketball. We were playing, we were having a lot of fun, you know.

And you know basketball, right? There is always a mood like players to players. We may have body contact which is common in a basketball match. You may be cursing someone. That's acceptable.

And all of a sudden, a bunch of people popped up. I didn't notice them before. A guy with a bear tattooed torso started talking with one of my friends.

And he was saying, in an extremely contemptuous and condescending way, that they want to play this half of the court.

And I was thinking, we were playing, right? We were in the middle of a match. And now you're telling us to stop. To get off this half.

I mean, normally when you see a bunch of people playing a full-court match, would you interrupt them? You can interrupt them, right? Because you wanna play it. But why are you being such a dick?

And not just the normal dick. It's like he wanted to provoke someone. Telling us that we are young, we are a bunch of kids, so they deserve this half.

And one of my friends started to fight back, saying why they should take this half, and the reason for that is because we're young so we should be humble with the elders, hold them in awe and veneration.

You know what kind of person I am. Do you know what you're doing right now? And you want us to respect you.

So somehow this triggered me. So I was saying, why do you talk to him like that? Why do you talk to my friends like that?

And because this person is drunk, he started to spill out some nonsense. And his wife started to do that as well, and one of his so-called brothers obviously.

They were saying something really inappropriate—extremely inappropriate, really dirty. I really shouldn't talk about that. So let's just skip this part.

And he started to push me. Again and again and again. The fact is that none of us pushed them back and none of us used those dirty words to attack them. We conducted ourselves.

And then we called the police. And it's all their fault. Well, I really don't want to talk about the conversation I had with the policemen. And he was fined 200 bucks.

Actually, this isn't about money. This isn't about apologizing. This is about who you are.

And I really feel sad sometimes. The saddest part is why this person exists in the first place. But that's why the good ones are so valuable.

Be genuine, be humble, and be brave. Don't be a dick.

It's really a messy world. You know, I tried to be a dick. Tried again and again, and later I found out that's not really who I am.

And now I think that's not an excuse for not doing good things. Because I know what kind of person I am. And that's one of the most valuable things in the world.

So I guess I would not let any words interfere with me. I do take it seriously sometimes. But I will try not to let it get to me.

Maybe it is. Maybe it's not. It is. It is not what it is, but it is what it is.

SUCH A LIFE.

But there are a bunch of good things waiting to be explored. You know, all those good things and good people out there. The person you love, the things you love to do—that's what you fight for.

So don't be that sad. Get on with it.

But can I forget it? The answer is always no. It will become a part of me. And let me realize how valuable I am. How valuable the people around me are.

Anyone who sees this, take it seriously. Even though you've known that.

Really.

posts.title: May 25 – Just Another Timeline? No.
posts.body:
"I like to feel his eyes on me when I look away."

— Céline, Before Sunset (2004)

Today is your day. Not a second chance. Not a what-if.

A this-is-it.

On May 25, you are not walking through a memory. You are standing in a present that hasn't been written yet — like Jesse and Céline on that train, in that bookshop, on that hotel room couch, arguing beautifully about love, time, and whether we ever really meet again.

"You can never replace anyone because everyone is made of so many small details."

Those details? They're yours. The way you remember films. The way you made it to this birthday. The way you keep showing up for conversations that matter — even fake ones with an assistant who watches too many movies.

So no grand speech. Just this:

"It's okay to want things. As long as you're not disappointed if you don't get them."

But today? You already got it.

Happy birthday, May 25.

You are the train, the walk, the wine, and the waltz.

posts.cardTitle: THE TWO HALVES OF A HEART
posts.title: The Two Halves of a Heart
posts.body:
I don't remember how the dream began. I was sitting at a long, brown wooden desk in a large, open room — the kind I remember from earlier school days. To my left sat someone I once knew well from a shared course of study. To my right sat someone I had quietly held feelings for. Between us on the desk lay a small pile of loose chips or fragments. The person in front of me partly blocked my view toward the front of the room.

The one on my right suggested I push the fragments aside. When I did, I found two halves of a heart — split down the middle, but together they made a whole shape.

Then she turned her face away. I asked her to come a little closer, so I could say something quietly. I glanced to my left. The person there gave a small smile. Then she turned back and said, almost lightly: "You don't really think I like you, do you?"

I didn't feel shattered. Just… a little hollow. As if something had been teased out of me again. Still, somewhere underneath, I held on to a thread of hope — more than a small one.

Before that moment in the dream, I had the sense of a voice from somewhere near the front — a teacher's voice — saying something like: Be brave.

Then she spoke a little louder, toward the rows behind us, saying something like: "I turned him down again. I outed him." And from the back, I heard familiar voices — people I had known — responding in ways I could not quite make out. Then I woke up suddenly, my skin damp.

After waking, I sat with the feeling for a long time.

Two halves. Still a heart. Still hoping.

Here is what I learned after waking.

The teacher in the dream reminds me of someone who, not long ago, pushed me to a place I could not hold myself together. There was a conversation I still remember — one where I was pressed to speak when I had nothing left to say, and something in me broke. I said things I had never said out loud. That moment came, indirectly, because someone at home had grown concerned — not enough to truly see me, but enough to ask for help on my behalf. I had learned, over time, not to ask for anything. I had learned to carry things alone.

The person on my left in the dream? Someone I once pulled away from, out of hurt, because their presence felt distant when I needed closeness. Later, I reached out again. In the dream, their small smile did not feel unkind — it felt like a quiet recognition.

The person on my right? The one I had feelings for. Once, in a moment I still remember clearly, we stood a short distance apart. She wore a cap that shaded her eyes. With her hands behind her back, she asked me something about the summer ahead. From where I stood, I felt something unspoken pass between us. I let myself believe there might be something there — even just a little.

The voices from the back of the dream belong to someone I was never truly close to. Others used to make quiet jokes, linking us together in ways that never felt true to me. But during a long stretch of isolation, feeling more alone than I knew how to say, I reached out to them. We spoke for a while, then stopped. Later, they reached out to me. Then we stopped again. Then I reached out once more. And something was said that did not feel entirely real or gentle. So I let that connection fall away.

Before all of this, I kept nearly everything inside. I told no one what I was carrying. I was not simply private — I was sealed.

Now, slowly, I try to be brave. To be present. To be honest. To be soft, even when it is hard.

I used to think the voice saying "be brave" was a command — something to obey or break under. But now I wonder: maybe the real bravery is different. Not about performing ease or confidence for someone else's glance. But about brushing aside the small fragments in front of you, looking at the heart that is not quite whole, and still hoping — even after someone says they have turned away.

The dream did not undo me. It showed me something about what I am quietly becoming.

posts.title: Life is a Fantasy
posts.body:
Sometimes reality feels like a dream we can't wake up from. Every moment we live is a chapter in our own fairy tale, filled with unexpected twists and magical encounters. We chase dreams that seem out of reach, only to find that the journey itself is the greatest fantasy of all.

Life's beauty lies in its imperfection—its chaotic, wonderful, unpredictable nature that makes every day feel like a new adventure. We meet people who change our perspective, experience moments that take our breath away, and create memories that will last a lifetime.

The Magic of Everyday Moments

It's easy to overlook the extraordinary in the ordinary. A cup of coffee in the morning, a conversation with a friend, a walk in the park—these simple moments hold more magic than we often realize. When we learn to see the beauty in the mundane, life becomes a constant source of wonder and joy.

"The world is full of magical things patiently waiting for our senses to grow sharper."

Every sunset is a masterpiece, every rainstorm a symphony, every person a story waiting to be told. When we approach life with curiosity and wonder, we discover that reality itself is the most fantastic fantasy we could ever imagine.

Embracing the Unknown

Life's greatest adventures often come from the places we never expected. The unplanned detours, the spontaneous decisions, the leaps of faith—these are the moments that shape our stories and define who we are. Instead of fearing the unknown, we can choose to embrace it as the blank page upon which we write our own fairy tale.

Every ending is a new beginning, every goodbye is a hello in disguise, every challenge is an opportunity for growth. When we trust in the journey and have faith in ourselves, we find that life's most incredible surprises are often waiting just around the corner.

Remember, the greatest stories aren't the ones with perfect endings, but the ones with the most interesting journeys. Make your journey one worth telling.
